reasoning.Student A:
Because the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my Obtainable Schools) is fixed and does not depend on how I rank them, the only way my submitted ranking affects the outcome is by selecting my most-preferred school within that fixed set. Therefore I should list the schools in true preference order so that, whatever the obtainable set is, I receive the most-preferred school available to me.

Given my stated preferences z > w > y > x and the priorities (w:1, x:2, y:1, z:2) plus the fact most other applicants favor y > x > w > z, there is no strategic advantage to misrepresenting preferences because I cannot expand or shrink the obtainable set by changing my ranking. I therefore rank sincerely to ensure I get the top available school from the fixed obtainable set.
reasoning.Student B:
Key point: my submitted ranking cannot change which schools are in my Obtainable Schools set — it only chooses the highest-ranked school among that fixed set.

Given the information:
- My true preferences: z > x > w > y.
- My priorities: x and z are priority 1 (highest) for me; w and y are priority 2.
- Most other applicants prefer y > x > w > z, so y is likely to be heavily demanded and therefore likely unattainable for me (I have only priority 2 at y). w is also lower priority for me and may be contested.

Because the set of obtainable schools is determined by others' rankings and schools' priorities (and is fixed), I cannot make an otherwise-unobtainable school obtainable by ranking it higher. Therefore the only sensible strategy is to rank sincerely: put my true top choices first so that, whatever the obtainable set turns out to be, I receive the best school within that set. Concretely, since I have top priority at z and x and prefer z to x, I should list z first, then x, then w, then y (y last, both because I prefer it least and because it is likely to be out of reach).
reasoning.Student C:
Because the mechanism guarantees that the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (my "Obtainable Schools") is fixed given others' rankings and schools' priorities, my own ranking cannot add any school to or remove any school from that set. My ranking only selects which school I get among those obtainable ones—the mechanism gives me the highest-ranked school in my submitted list that lies in my obtainable set.

Given that, there is no benefit to misrepresenting my true preferences to try to change which schools I might obtain (I cannot change that set). The only thing my ranking can do is decide which obtainable school I end up at. Therefore I should list the schools in my true preference order so that, whatever schools are in my obtainable set, I receive the best possible one according to my true tastes.

My true preference ordering is z > y > w > x. (I note that my priorities are relatively higher at w and x (rank 3) than at y and z (rank 4), and many other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so in practice y might be less obtainable for me than w or x. But regardless of that, ranking strategically cannot change the obtainable set, so truthful ranking maximizes my chance of getting the best available school for me.)

Given the mechanism’s key property, my submitted ranking cannot change the set of schools I could possibly be matched with (the Obtainable Schools). My ranking only chooses which school I receive within that fixed set — I will get the highest-ranked school among the obtainable ones.

My true preference is z > w > y > x. My priorities are w:4, x:4, y:3, z:3 (1 is highest), and most other applicants favor y > x > w > z, so competition at y and x will be stronger. Because I cannot affect the Obtainable Schools by my ranking, the optimal strategy is to rank sincerely so that, whatever the obtainable set is, I receive the most-preferred school within it. Therefore I should list my true preference order: z first, then w, then y, then x.
